lesson.title: Eight Bits, One Byte: The Unit Data Is Actually Measured In
lesson.summary: A byte groups bits, in modern practice almost always eight of them, into a single unit large enough to represent a character or a small number, and it is the unit nearly all networking specifications actually measure things in.
lesson.body:
A single bit, a lone 0 or 1, cannot represent much on its own. It can distinguish between exactly two states, which is enough for a light switch but nowhere near enough to represent a letter of the alphabet, a color, or a number of any real size. A byte solves this by grouping bits together, and in essentially all modern computing and networking, a byte means exactly eight bits. Eight bits gives 2 to the power of 8, which is 256, distinct combinations, which is enough to represent the entire ASCII character set, originally defined using just 7 of those bits for 128 characters, or a single color channel's intensity ranging from 0 to 255, or a great many other small but genuinely useful quantities.

There is a subtlety networking documents care about that everyday usage glosses over. Historically, not every computer architecture agreed that a byte meant 8 bits. Some older systems used 6-bit, 7-bit, or 9-bit bytes, which is exactly the kind of ambiguity a shared protocol cannot tolerate, since two devices need to agree precisely on how many bits make up one unit of data. For this reason, RFC documents and other formal networking specifications typically use the word octet instead of byte, defined unambiguously as exactly 8 bits regardless of what any particular computer's native word size happens to be. You will see "octet" throughout IETF documents like RFC 791, which defines IP, for exactly this reason.

This distinction between bits and bytes causes a genuinely common real-world mistake worth working through concretely. Internet connection speeds are almost always advertised in bits per second, so a "100 Mbps" connection means 100 megabits per second. File sizes and download progress bars, on the other hand, are almost always shown in bytes, so a 1,200 megabyte file is 1,200 megabytes, not megabits. Since one byte equals eight bits, that same 100 Mbps connection can theoretically transfer at most 100 divided by 8, or 12.5 megabytes per second. Downloading that 1,200 megabyte file at the connection's theoretical maximum would therefore take roughly 1,200 divided by 12.5, or about 96 seconds, not the 12 seconds someone gets if they mistakenly treat the advertised 100 Mbps as 100 megabytes per second.

Bytes are also the unit that essentially every networking data structure covered in the coming chapters is actually measured in. A standard Ethernet frame can carry a payload of up to 1,500 bytes. A typical IPv4 header is 20 bytes long. A TCP header is also normally 20 bytes. None of these numbers are arbitrary, and none of them would mean anything if the two communicating devices did not first agree on exactly how many bits constitute one byte.

Byte is the natural chunk size that both hardware and software are built around: memory is addressed byte by byte, files are measured in bytes, and every header field in every protocol discussed from here forward will be described as being some specific number of bytes long. Keeping the bit-versus-byte distinction straight, and remembering that eight of the former make one of the latter, is what makes the more detailed structures in the following chapters actually legible.
